incorrect_claims.claim: Fence: gain does not add energy. A directional antenna sends the same power into a narrower beam.
incorrect_claims.correction: "Fence:" is a stray label, probably left over from a template or prompt. It means nothing to students. The bullet should read: "Gain does not create energy: a directional antenna focuses the same power into a narrower beam."
The source says "Wi-Fi 5/6 GHz". Without "GHz", the label reads as the Wi-Fi 5 and Wi-Fi 6 generations, not the 5 and 6 GHz bands.

incorrect_claims.claim: Note that Maxwell's 1865 equations to 2019 is about 150 years; the module's own takeaway says about 120, so quote the dates, not that number.
incorrect_claims.correction: The arithmetic is right (1865 to 2019 is 154 years), but the note tells the lecturer to ignore the module's own takeaway when it should just restate it. It also leaves out the takeaway's main point about efficiency. Better wording: 'more than a century'.

incorrect_claims.claim: At high SNR, which raises capacity more: bandwidth or SNR?
incorrect_claims.correction: The module asks about doubling bandwidth versus doubling SNR. The slide drops 'doubling', but the answer slide says 'Doubling bandwidth', so the question and answer no longer match.

incorrect_claims.claim: Summary: nine ideas to take away
incorrect_claims.correction: The slide shows three rows. Summary point 4 (real channels reflect, diffract, scatter and fade; multipath is the main enemy) is missing, so it does not show nine ideas.

invented_claims.claim: A high-gain antenna is not an amplifier: it concentrates the same power into a narrower beam, like a torch with a focused lens.
Ask: why does a home router not use a dish? Because the signal has to go in all directions to reach phones around the room.
Ask: why is the 1G row a frequency split? Because each call got its own frequency channel.
It is the promise for the next 45 minutes.

ui_issues.issue: In the Maxwell column, 'electromagnetic' runs into the Hertz column and overlaps 'radio waves'.
The band boxes are cramped. 'Wi-Fi 5/6, radar' runs past the SHF box border, and the range labels touch the box edges. The text is small for a projector.
Each answer has both a number and a bullet ('1. • 6 cm'). The list is also pushed left of the title margin.
The image placeholder caption sits on top of the decorative concentric lines, which makes it harder to read.
The image placeholder caption sits on top of the decorative concentric lines, which makes it harder to read.
The handover arc is a tiny curve near the A/B border and is easy to miss. It does not clearly show a user moving between cells.
The question headings wrap into narrow columns of 4–5 lines while the left half of the slide is empty.

major_mistakes: Slide 9 shows the stray label 'Fence:' in bold on a content bullet. Students would see it on screen and it would embarrass the lecturer.
Slide 3's timeline text overlaps between columns ('electromagnetic' runs into the Hertz column).
strengths: All the worked numbers match the source: λ examples, the dBm table, FSPL ≈ 80 dB, the link budget (−56 dBm, 34 dB margin), Shannon ≈ 199 Mbit/s, the Doppler shift of 200 Hz, and the quiz answers.

It follows the module's sections in order, and facts left off the slides (the full path-loss exponent table, ITU/FCC/Ofcom, the ISM and 6 GHz bands, the GSM/Bluetooth/LTE dates) are kept in the speaker notes.
The speaker notes are strong. They give click-by-click cues, questions to ask the room, and arithmetic to work aloud, and they do not just repeat the slide.
The animated link-budget chain and the bits-per-symbol chart show the key arithmetic clearly. The frequency-reuse hex grid uses a valid 3-cell pattern.
It meets the requirements: 29 slides, quiz then answers then summary at the end, and the checker passes with 0 issues.
structured_output.verdict: This is a solid deck that follows the module closely, gets the numbers right and has excellent speaker notes. Fix three things before teaching from it tomorrow: the stray 'Fence:' label on slide 9, the overlapping timeline text on slide 3, and the double markers on the answers slide. There are four animated diagrams (wave, spectrum, link-budget chain, hex grid). The ideas that would gain most from a picture have none: a QAM constellation, multipath or fading, and FDMA/TDMA/OFDMA. The deck also has no Part 1 or Part 3 section dividers to match the three-question structure.
